hook.text: You breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. Inside your cells, the real story unfolds.

buildup.text: Glucose and oxygen enter the mitochondria. A chain of reactions breaks glucose apart.

discovery.text: The process yields up to 36 ATP molecules from a single glucose molecule.

twist.text: Most ATP comes from the electron transport chain, not from breaking glucose directly.

climax.text: Without oxygen, cells switch to fermentation and produce far less energy.

punchline.text: Breathing feeds your cells, not just your lungs.

quiz.question: How many ATP molecules can one glucose molecule yield?

details.summary: Cellular respiration is the process by which cells break down glucose using oxygen to produce ATP energy. It occurs in three stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
details.whyItMatters: Cellular respiration is how every cell in your body extracts energy from food. It produces 36 to 38 ATP molecules per glucose molecule, making it far more efficient than fermentation and essential for complex multicellular life.
takeaways: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate, yielding 2 ATP without oxygen
The Krebs cycle extracts electrons and produces CO2 in mitochondria
Oxidative phosphorylation produces the bulk of ATP using an electron chain

faq.question: Why do we need oxygen to produce energy?
faq.answer: Oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain. Without it, the chain stalls and the cell cannot efficiently produce ATP through oxidative phosphorylation. Cells revert to fermentation, which yields only 2 ATP per glucose.

faq.question: Where does the CO2 we exhale come from?
faq.answer: The CO2 you breathe out is produced during the Krebs cycle when carbon atoms from glucose are stripped of their electrons and released. Each glucose molecule produces six CO2 molecules during complete cellular respiration.
